Centuries-old dust hints at a dying stars last-minute chaos

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The mix of elements that ends up in planets — even people — can hinge on a final shake-up inside a dying star, upcoming space observations suggest.
  • A team of researchers studied Cassiopeia A, a glowing cloud of gas and dust left behind by an exploding star.
  • "What's amazing is that the dust, which we are testing hundreds of years after the explosion, tells us about what happened to the star potentially only hours before it exploded," said Dan Milisavljevic, a Purdue University professor and co-author of the study, in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The mix of elements that ends up in planets — even people — can hinge on a final shake-up inside a dying star, upcoming space observations suggest.

A team of researchers studied Cassiopeia A, a glowing cloud of gas and dust left behind by an exploding star. Using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope, the astronomers could parse out clumps within the 350-year-old cloud and analyze their compositions. The debris from the explosion, called a supernova, is still racing outward in space at about 11 million mph.

"What's amazing is that the dust, which we are testing hundreds of years after the explosion, tells us about what happened to the star potentially only hours before it exploded," said Dan Milisavljevic, a Purdue University professor and co-author of the study, in a statement.

In a recent development, supernova explosions forge and scatter many of the heavy elements that later get recycled into upcoming stars and worlds. Computer models have long predicted that a star's inner layers could merge before it explodes. But scientists don't fully understand why and how some stars go through this violent process. The new study, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, adds evidence that it happened in Cassiopeia A, giving astronomers a way to peer inside a star that hasn't existed for centuries.

According to recent reports, A massive star builds up in layers, like an onion, with each shell fusing a different element. When the star explodes, some of that material cools into dust. Each layer makes its own kind of dust, so the grains, smaller than the width of a human hair, keep a record of what sat where inside the star.

As the layers merge, they can change the mix of elements the blast flings out, mentioned Tea Temim, lead author of the study.

"So, for example, the oxygen- and carbon-burning shells in a star merge together and change the structure of the star significantly," said Temim, a research scientist at Columbia University in Upcoming York. "And that would then change the chemical abundances that you would see after a supernova explosion.".

In a recent development, to look for evidence, the team pointed Webb at three spots in Cassiopeia A, or Cas A, that NASA's retired Spitzer Space Telescope had previously flagged. Spitzer saw the debris as a blur, with light from many clumps mixed together. Webb's sharper view separates individual clumps, each roughly the size of our solar system, so the team could study them one at a time.

Recent findings suggest that one clump held mostly silica dust, the main ingredient in most sand. Another held mostly carbon dust. The third sits in a feature nicknamed the Green Monster, and its dust is rich in magnesium and silicon. That material didn't come from the blast at all; rather, the star shed it before it exploded.

Industry observers note that the researchers then compared their measurements with existing computer models of exploding stars. Only the models in which the star's layers had merged could reproduce both the silica-rich and the carbon-rich debris. A wider Webb dust map demonstrates signs of the merger across much of the cloud.

The team cautions that those models are incomplete. Researchers will need more detailed 3D simulations — and Webb observations of more spots in the cloud — to confirm the merger.

This approach also could help astronomers make sense of supernovas in other galaxies.

"I think it's remarkable that we can watch these changes and understand what they mean from thousands of light-years away," Milisavljevic remarked.

Lava-drenched and menacing, it's wholly unlike the forging of any of the other rings of power we've seen onscreen in the series so far. For showrunners McKay and J.D. Payne, that was the goal.

"We wanted it to be more than he's making a weapon or a magical object," McKay said. "He's changing as a character forever. The world is changing in this moment.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple is about to launch several new gadgets in a red colorway, reports say.

According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, Apple will launch a red HomePod mini 2 and AirPods Max, likely on December 1, which is World AIDS Day.

Sources indicate that the new gadgets will be part of Apple's support for Product(Red), a brand that partners with private companies to raise awareness of HIV/AIDS. Apple has supported Product(Red) for two decades, typically by launching red versions of its gadgets. A part of the proceeds from the sale of these products goes to Global Fund, a non-profit organization that fights HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria.

Industry observers note that the upcoming HomePod mini 2 will reportedly have a red mesh exterior, and the AirPods Max 2 are likely to have a silver finish, white mesh ear cushions and headband, and a red Digital Crown. If the amount of red on the AirPods sounds disappointing, it's worth remembering that the AirPods Max 2 right now don't come in silver or white, so these new ones should feel quite fresh in the lineup. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

If the report is accurate, this would mark the first new Product(Red) releases from Apple in three years; the last one was the red Apple Watch Series 9, which released in 2023.

Gurman later added that Apple will also launch two Product(Red) accessories: A red AirPods Wrist Strap and red Apple Watch Sport Band.

In a recent development, finally, 9to5Mac added that Apple has also developed a Product(Red) version of its AirTag tracker. It's unclear whether it will launch alongside the other gadgets mentioned above.

According to recent reports, none of these gadgets are likely to have any added upcoming functionality aside from the change in color. Prices are also likely to remain identical to the standard color versions of the same products.

To help you get the details straight and gear up to shop at Walmart on Black Friday 2026, here's everything you need to know, including when stores open, the best deals already live, ad highlights, and how to get early access.

Walmart Early Black Friday Sale: Nov. 12 to Nov. 15.

Walmart Black Friday Sale: Nov. 23 at 12:01 a.m. ET to Nov. 29 (online only Nov. 23 to Nov. 26, in stores at 6 a.m. local time on Nov. 27).

Walmart Cyber Monday Sale: Nov. 30 at 12:01 a.m. ET to Dec. 2 (online only).

Walmart+ members have access to "hot deal drops" starting 12:01 a.m. ET on Nov. 23. According to the superstore, any remaining hot deal drops are open to all customers starting 12:01 a.m. ET.

If you love your current mattress but hate waking up drenched in sweat — or arguing with your partner over the bedroom thermostat — this Orion Sleep System deal lets you upgrade your bed's temperature without buying a whole upcoming mattress. For Black Friday, Orion is taking $600 off every size of its smart cooling and heating mattress cover system, with no monthly subscription fee.

The system comes with two main parts: a thin Smart Cover (available in softer or firmer comfort options with a breathable 60% polyester and 40% bamboo top knit) that stretches over any standard mattress between 10 and 18 inches deep like a fitted sheet, and an award-winning, oak-topped bedside Control Tower that plugs into a single outlet.

The Control Tower circulates temperature-controlled water through anti-leak, tear-resistant tubing inside the cover, maintaining a temperature between 50 and 113 degrees Fahrenheit. Because it uses dual-zone control, each side of the bed can run its own temperature — so one person can sleep at 73 degrees while the other stays cozy at 82 degrees.

Sources indicate that you can set automated schedules in the Orion app, so your bed cools down before you get in, drops lower for deep sleep, and gently warms up before your alarm goes off. There is also a Hot Flash mode that drops your side's temperature before easing back to your schedule, plus a Quiet mode that turns down the tower's sound at night.

Industry observers note that built-in sensors track your heart rate, breathing rate, HRV, and movement without making you wear anything to bed, delivering sleep insights each morning. You only need to top off the tower's water once or twice a year with a purification tablet. And while the cover itself is spot-clean only, you just put your regular fitted sheet over it and wash it as usual.

Recent findings suggest that if you want a little extra help dialing in your settings, you can add an at-home Sleep Disruption Test (a one-night sensor patch and a quick call with a Sleep Advisor) to find your best starting temperature before you commit. You can also sync the app with Apple Health or Google Health Connect, or pay extra for Orion Intelligence — an optional AI add-on that adjusts your temperature schedule automatically based on your sleep and breathing habits, while keeping all core features subscription-free.

The system comes with two main parts: a thin Smart Cover (available in softer or firmer comfort options with a breathable 60% polyester and 40% bamboo top knit) that stretches over any standard mattress between 10 and 18 inches deep like a fitted sheet, and an award-winning, oak-topped bedside Control Tower that plugs into a single outlet.

The Control Tower circulates temperature-controlled water through anti-leak, tear-resistant tubing inside the cover, maintaining a temperature between 50 and 113 degrees Fahrenheit. Because it uses dual-zone control, each side of the bed can run its own temperature — so one person can sleep at 73 degrees while the other stays cozy at 82 degrees.

Recent findings suggest that you can set automated schedules in the Orion app, so your bed cools down before you get in, drops lower for deep sleep, and gently warms up before your alarm goes off. There is also a Hot Flash mode that drops your side's temperature before easing back to your schedule, plus a Quiet mode that turns down the tower's sound at night.

Sources indicate that built-in sensors track your heart rate, breathing rate, HRV, and movement without making you wear anything to bed, delivering sleep insights each morning. You only need to top off the tower's water once or twice a year with a purification tablet. And while the cover itself is spot-clean only, you just put your regular fitted sheet over it and wash it as usual.

Sources indicate that if you want a little extra help dialing in your settings, you can add an at-home Sleep Disruption Test (a one-night sensor patch and a quick call with a Sleep Advisor) to find your best starting temperature before you commit. You can also sync the app with Apple Health or Google Health Connect, or pay extra for Orion Intelligence — an optional AI add-on that adjusts your temperature schedule automatically based on your sleep and breathing habits, while keeping all core features subscription-free.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If it feels like everyone and their dog is watching or streaming Grand Theft Auto VI content, YouTube has the official numbers to prove it.

Sources indicate that in a blog post Tuesday, the manufacturer detailed the colossal online impact of Rockstar Games' critically acclaimed blockbuster, announcing that YouTube saw over 3.5 billion global views of videos with GTA 6 in the title on Nov. 19's release day.

To date, the Grand Theft Auto series has over 900 billion views of related content on YouTube, according to the data, with videos specifically about GTA 6 gaining 40 billion views before release day.

Recent findings suggest that along with YouTubers, streamers across Twitch and Kick broke streaming records with GTA 6 content on launch day. Data from streaming analytics platform Streams Charts noted Twitch saw 2.50 million views while Kick had 1.31 million (the platform clocked YouTube at 3.22 million views, less than the company now reports), marking a reported total of 7.91 million concurrent GTA 6 launch day viewers.

In context, the 24-hour record for most views on one YouTube clip remains with K-pop superstars BTS, whose 2021 "Butter" video saw 108.2 million views in one day, smashing their own 101.1 million-view first-day record for previous single "Dynamite.".

However, GTA 6 can claim the record for most views in a 24-hour debut of a non-music video for the very first trailer released in Dec. 2023: 93 million views in 24 hours.

To mark the streaming news, YouTube added a few GTA 6 themed features to YouTube Live including onscreen Wanted Stars (the stars that pop-up in game if there's police heat on protagonists Jason and Lucia), and a Shorts effect that lets creators use Vice City backgrounds.

Turns out viewers can't get enough of watching others reap the spoils of Leonida — and if you're looking for the best streamers to watch playing GTA 6, Mashable's got you covered.

Is there an adjustable mattress that also cools? How active temperature control works.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that TL;DR: Yes — beds like Sleep Number's ClimateCool and Climate360 pair adjustable firmness with active temperature control on each side, and both are discounted up to 25% through Dec.
  • Anyone shopping for a cooler night's sleep eventually runs into the same two questions: Is there an adjustable mattress that actively cools you down, and how does built-in temperature control work alongside adjustable firmness?
  • If you want to test one out for yourself, Sleep Number's Black Friday sale runs through Dec.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that TL;DR: Yes — beds like Sleep Number's ClimateCool and Climate360 pair adjustable firmness with active temperature control on each side, and both are discounted up to 25% through Dec. 7 for Black Friday.

Anyone shopping for a cooler night's sleep eventually runs into the same two questions: Is there an adjustable mattress that actively cools you down, and how does built-in temperature control work alongside adjustable firmness? As it turns out, you can get both in the same bed — and the way it works is completely different from standard "cooling" mattresses.

If you want to test one out for yourself, Sleep Number's Black Friday sale runs through Dec. 7, with up to 25% off its lineup — including deep discounts on its active-cooling Climate Collection.

In a recent development, most mattresses advertised as cooling rely on passive materials such as gel-infused foam, breathable fabrics, or open-cell airflow layers. Those materials feel cool when you first lie down, and a bedroom fan can help move air across your skin, but passive toppers and covers eventually absorb your body heat and warm up — while a fan cannot reach the heat trapped beneath your back.

Active temperature mattresses solve this by building motorized airflow channels directly into the bed to pull warm air away from your body all night long.

In mattresses like the Sleep Number Climate Collection, the active temperature system sits right alongside adjustable firmness. Instead of traditional metal springs, the bed uses split air chambers underneath layers of supportive foam, letting you dial in your preferred firmness on each side at any time.

Built-in sensors also track your movement while you sleep — so if you roll from your back onto your side, the air chambers automatically soften or firm up under your hips and shoulders to keep your spine level, without interrupting your cooling settings. At the same time, sensors quietly track your heart rate, breathing, and movement in the background (no smartwatch required), rolling everything into a morning SleepIQ score from 1 to 100 in the app.

Because both the air chambers and the temperature vents are split down the middle, each side of the bed works independently. On the Sleep Number ClimateCool, a programmable airflow system within a 1.25-inch foam layer pulls excess heat away, lowering the temperature of each side by up to 15 degrees, and it works alongside a breathable cover and 3.75 inches of temperature-balancing comfort foam.

Sources indicate that the Sleep Number Climate360 adds active warming into the mix — spanning a 30-degree range from cooler to warmer on each side — and includes 52% more built-in cooling materials plus a smart adjustable base. Both models also run pre-set temperature programs in the app that automatically shift through the night, such as warming your feet at bedtime on the Climate360 before kicking on active cooling during deep sleep.

In a recent development, struggling to sleep? You might fall into one of these categories:.

Chronic hot sleepers — If you routinely wake up sweating, continuous active airflow keeps heat from building up under your body the way gel toppers and foam pads eventually do.

Couples with different temperature preferences — Because firmness and temperature are set separately on each side, one person can sleep cool on a firm surface while the other stays warm on a softer setup (on the Climate360, one side can actively cool while the other warms).

People with night sweats or temperature swings — Pre-set overnight schedules adjust as you sleep — cooling you down when your temperature spikes or gently warming the bed before you wake up.

If you sleep alone, don't overheat, and already stay comfortable with a bedroom fan or breathable sheets, there is no real need to spend thousands on built-in airflow.

Both models in the Sleep Number smart beds collection are engineered for a 25-year lifespan, come with a 100-night home trial, and are HSA/FSA-eligible — though keep in mind that home delivery and setup fees are non-refundable, and return pickup fees apply if you send the bed back.

Grab your preferred Climate model at Sleep Number before the Black Friday discounts wrap up, and put an end to middle-of-the-night overheating for good.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Google debuted its inaugural screenless fitness tracker, the Fitbit Air, it introduced distraction-free health monitoring to its wearables lineup at a reasonable price — but that also meant sacrificing notifications and notable alerts altogether, which, in certain circumstances, can be life-saving.

It's a very simple device, offering limited vibration alerts for alarms, but it lacks support for incoming calls and has very limited customization options, so third-party developers are stepping in.

Sharing the news on Reddit (see below), the minds behind the new Android app Cuff have created a way to give your Fitbit Air the ability to receive alerts for incoming calls via the device's vibration motor. By communicating with your wearable over Bluetooth, the app gives you the freedom to enable alerts for individual apps, create custom vibration patterns, and even receive call alerts from specific people in your contacts list. For iOS consumers, Airbuzz is a similar alternative.

Recent findings suggest that sounds handy, doesn't it? But it doesn't draw the line there.

Sources indicate that cuff's personalized alerts are just the start. As detailed in the developer's Reddit post, Cuff supports Stackable Widgets, which let you combine multiple widgets into a single one, eliminating the hassle of creating and relying on separate spaces for each health metric.

Industry observers note that but the idea behind the app, the developer indicates, comes from their longing for an alert feature that's triggered every hour when no movement is detected. Unlike other flagship fitness trackers, this is a small but handy feature left out of the Fitbit Air's roster of capabilities. I have it enabled on my Apple Watch, and it does a solid job of getting me up and moving after sitting at my desk for long intervals.

Sources indicate that food tracking is another tool that Cuff has brought to the Fitbit Air, which the developer says isn't as polished in the Google Health app. There's also a dedicated section that gives you a comprehensive overview of your calorie deficits and surpluses per week, ensuring smoother, more reliable progress-tracking. Additionally, Cuff can track accumulated sleep deficit over a week's period to show you exactly how much sleep you're missing.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Sources indicate that when it comes to custom alerts on screenless fitness trackers, I can how some would view the notion as slightly counteractive. If devices like the Fitbit Air are rooted in the goal to eliminate distractions and digital screens, embedding notifications kind of defeats the object.

That said, giving users choices and options is a different matter. Yes, enlisting apps like Cuff opens the notification floodgate, but at least the personalization touch provides some sort of barrier that allows you to draw the line somewhere. For some, incoming calls and other minor alerts, especially from family members, are just as vital as basic health pattern monitoring.

#3912. Not Just Nvidia: Inside Team Trump’s Takeover of Intel

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1920 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Not Just Nvidia: Inside Team Trump’s Takeover of Intel

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1920 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your firm.
  • Sources indicate that do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit.
  • According to recent reports, shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your firm. Right now. Or else.

Sources indicate that do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms on Friday.”.

According to recent reports, shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors. But the Trump administration official “noted that rejection will have consequences that [Shapiro] cannot predict.”.

According to recent reports, days later, the board gave the administration what it wanted. “It is my Great Honor to report that the United States of America now fully owns and controls 10% of INTEL,” Donald Trump posted to his social platform. “The United States paid nothing for these Shares, and the Shares are now valued at approximately $11 Billion Dollars. This is a great Deal for America.”.

According to recent reports, president Trump was similarly jubilant on Monday, announcing that he had “convinced” Nvidia’s board of directors to rehire chief executive Jensen Huang. The proclamation was a shock. But it wasn’t entirely without precedent.

It has been revealed that fifteen months earlier, the Trump administration had interfered with the leadership decisions at another major chipmaker, court documents allege. Then, as now, allegations swirled that the manufacturer’s CEO was too close to China. Then, as now, the Trump administration dealt itself into the company’s financial future.

It’s part of a broader shift within the government in general and the Commerce Department in particular, a former member of that department tells WIRED. Out are old metrics “like creating jobs or the US being more competitive or owning more of the market share,” this ex-Trump administration official notes. When dealing with private companies, a single overriding concern is: “Are you going to give back to the government in cash?”.

Recent findings suggest that documents unredacted as part of a shareholder’s lawsuit against Intel’s board show how far the administration has been willing to go to get what it wants. The lawsuit’s allegations were previously reported by WP Intelligence.

“The Board, operating under the shadow of the President’s threats,” the lawsuit alleges, “caved to the government’s extortion.” A second case, asking for internal records, was filed in April by the same shareholder, Richard Paisner, against Nvidia.

In a recent development, “It's just straight-up coercion,” claims Scott Lincicome, a vice president at the libertarian Cato Institute. “The firm starts making decisions not based on what's best for the company in the short or long term, what's best for shareholders, but what's best for politics and what the government is demanding.”.

Sources indicate that “That's not what you want from any tech giant,” he adds. “When you're talking about the world's most innovative companies and these kinds of bleeding-edge technologies that have not only huge economic implications but national security ones, then that's a huge problem.”.

Representatives for Intel declined to comment for this story. The White House, Commerce Department, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.

In a recent development, the parallels between Nvidia’s government-assisted autogolpe and Intel’s alleged forced sale aren’t exact. In the Intel case, Trump all but accused the company’s boss of being compromised by Beijing; in the Nvidia situation, the president reportedly dismissed concerns from his own intelligence agencies about the executive’s connections to China. But both instances show a growing fusion of private enterprise and public office.

During the Biden administration, Intel won awards for up to $11 billion in government grants and contracts, much of it under the CHIPS Act, which was meant to help build semiconductor manufacturing and assembly plants in America and bolster domestic research.

Sources indicate that at the time, there was some grumbling inside the Commerce Department, which administered the CHIPS and Science Act grants, about funding what was seen as a “failing incumbent” in the semiconductor space, notes the former official. (Intel had, in recent years, fallen on hard times.) But by March 2025, Intel had received about $2.2 billion of the grants. That’s when President Trump told Congress that the CHIPS Act was “a horrible, horrible thing.” The rest of Intel’s money was put on hold, tied to hitting certain milestones, while the administration said it was renegotiating the deals.

The same month Lip-Bu Tan was hired as Intel’s new CEO. Soon after, his ties to China made him a Trump target, when Reuters reported that Tan had invested in “hundreds of Chinese tech firms,” some with connections to Beijing's military. Tan’s former firm, Cadence Design Systems, pleaded guilty to violating US sanctions by selling semiconductor designs to a restricted Chinese military university, and agreed to pay more than $140 million in fines. Tan was never personally charged, but the violations happened while he was the CEO.

Two weeks later, the president was watching Maria Bartiromo’s show on the Fox Business Network. It mentioned a letter a senator had sent Intel about the China ties. Trump posted, "The CEO of INTEL is highly CONFLICTED and must resign, immediately. There is no other solution to this problem.".

Tan went to the Oval Office on August 11 to see if there was, in fact, another solution. He got 40 minutes with the president, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

According to recent reports, tan claimed his experience in China was a strength, not a detriment. According to the book Regime Change, Tan argued that there was no way he could’ve known about every one of the deals his many companies made; Trump, who had his own sprawling business empire, surely knew what that was like. Tan promised to give up his holdings in China, according to a letter Tan shared with Intel’s board, and put any proceeds into a blind trust.

Sources indicate that “The primary goal was to eliminate any worries about Lip-Bu himself, his Cadence background and his investments with China,” according to a source with knowledge of the matter. But there were major financial concerns for Intel, too. “We had declining revenues and needed money.”.

Neither Tan’s letter, excerpted in the complaint, nor Trump’s social media posts praising the CEO after the meeting mentioned anything about giving the government a chunk of the company. Yet Trump later insisted that a deal had been cooked up right then and there. “He came in, he saw me, we talked for a while. I liked him a lot, I thought he was very good,” the president told the Wall Street Journal. “I stated, ‘You know what? I think the United States should be given 10% of Intel.’ And he said, ‘I would consider that.’”.

“I should’ve asked for more. It was so easy,” Trump later recalled.

According to the court filing’s review of Intel’s internal documents, Shapiro—a former partner at the Latest York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz—made a verbal offer on August 18. Ultimately, in exchange for the cut of Intel, the Trump administration would free up the $8.9 billion US government grants that it had already won. They wanted about a tenth of the tech giant’s stock for free, in exchange for Washington keeping the commitment it had already made.

Then came the call in which Shapiro insisted there was no room for negotiation. “The board needs to consider,” he remarked, according to Intel’s summary of his remarks included in the court documents, the “benefits of having a friend in this administration and what the administration can do to help Intel (including with customers).”.

Industry observers note that intel’s board met, and decided they hated the deal. “The economic terms that had been proposed [by] the Administration were not, in their current form, attractive to the firm,” minutes of the meeting, reprinted in the lawsuit, noted.

But they went ahead with it anyway. Paisner’s lawyers say in the court documents the board took the offer thrust forward by the administration. Intel’s attorneys disagree, arguing in their motion to dismiss that there was some back-and-forth deal-making, and it made the agreement more favorable to the tech giant. The grants became “immediately available” while “strategically aligning the interests of Intel’s stockholders and the US Government.”.

Industry observers note that on August 25, Lutnick released a video with Tan, sitting side-by-side on cushioned chairs. “I really look forward to have the US government be my shareholder,” Tan turned to Lutnick and said. “And we can work together and make Intel great again.”.

Inside the firm, the video was “a surprise to everyone,” according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter. Some employees joked that it was reminiscent of a “hostage video.”.

Sources indicate that not long after that, Nvidia—led by Tan’s friend Jensen Huang—made a $5 billion investment in Intel. “I love seeing their stock price go up, making the USA RICHER, AND RICHER,” Trump posted. “Who would not want to make deals like that?”.

According to recent reports, deals, plural. On the day Tan was hauled to the Oval Office, Trump confirmed that his administration had been negotiating separately with Huang. The Nvidia leader was beyond eager to sell more of his semiconductors to China. “And I mentioned, if I'm going to do that, I want you to pay us as a country something,’” Trump said. They settled on 15 percent of all sales of the H20 model chip. Months after that, they cut a second deal: a 25 percent bounty on sales of Nvidia’s even-more advanced H200 chips.

In their lawsuit against Nvidia, Paisner’s attorneys argue the surcharges amount to “unlawful taxes,” and that the board’s “decisions to enter into such agreements are the product of mismanagement and breaches of fiduciary duty.”.

It has been revealed that in court, NVIDIA’s lawyers insisted that the organization “did not enter into any illegal ‘agreement’ with the government but instead engaged with the government and stated that it would comply with federal regulations.” Moreover, the attorneys say Paisner is trying to make a political point, rather than a legal one. “When asked about his purpose in bringing this action,” they write, “Paisner was candid: ‘It’s to make a public point of how NVIDIA conducts itself.’”.

Industry observers note that the attorneys wrote this in May, months before Nvidia’s and Huang’s recent drama. Last week, board chair Harvey Jones mentioned on the company’s quarterly earnings call that it did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” citing his “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” (Not to mention mounting evidence that the company’s most sophisticated chips were making their way to China, in violation of US law.) But, according to The Latest York Times, after days of pressure from top administration officials, the company and the government essentially struck a deal Sunday night to reinstate Huang.

According to recent reports, “Don’t think for a second that politics ever play a role in this company, not even a little bit,” Huang said during his first company-wide meeting after rejoining the company, WIRED reported. “We are the most apolitical company. I don’t love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”.

Additional reporting by Lauren Goode.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: On Thanksgiving Day (Nov. 26), Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Costco, and most major retailers are closed all day, while select grocers (like Kroger, Wegmans, and Whole Foods) and drugstores (Walgreens and CVS) stay open with modified hours.

It has been revealed that whether you realized halfway through prepping dinner that you forgot the cranberry sauce or need an emergency prescription refill, finding an open store on Thanksgiving Day is trickier than it used to be. For the seventh straight year, almost every major big-box, warehouse, and department store — including Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Costco, Lowe's, and Kohl's — is keeping its doors locked all day on Thursday, Nov. 26.

In a recent development, that does not mean you are completely out of luck, though. A handful of grocery chains, drugstores, dollar stores, and outdoor retailers will stay open on Thanksgiving with modified holiday hours (mostly closing by mid-afternoon, often with their pharmacy counters shut).

We rounded up which stores are open and closed on Thanksgiving 2026 below so you don't waste a trip to an empty parking lot and can plan your Thursday errands accordingly.

If you need last-minute ingredients on Thursday morning, several major supermarket chains are staying open with shortened hours. Sources indicate that there's a current trend for deception games, partly driven by the popularity of TV's The Traitors. Chameleon sees a group of players take turn to describe a word or concept without actually saying it. But one player is actually the Chameleon and has to guess the word from the other players' clues — all while avoiding detection. It's a ridiculous amount of fun, and perfect for massive groups and players of all ages.

Catan is a veritable board game classic, and it's a great pick to snag while it's discounted. Three to four players settle a randomly laid-out island, collecting wood, brick, wool, grain, and ore to build roads, settlements, and cities. Games wrap up in about an hour to 90 minutes, and it's fairly easy to learn. And if you're tired of playing the same things over and over, Catan's modular board means no two games set up the same way. It's a significant upgrade from Monopoly that's suitable for the whole family.

The classics are classic for a reason. Mouse Trap has delighted kids and families for years, and nothing has changed after all this time. Indeed, it's as fiddly to set up as it ever was, but there's no denying the fun of setting the trap in motion. Kids will love the mechanics, parents will love the nostalgia. You can also find Black Friday discounts on other kids classics, including Connect 4, Battleship, and Candy Land.

Industry observers note that if you've ever wanted to get started with Dungeons & Dragons but didn't know how, this board game is the perfect introduction. It has a quick-start guide, player boards for the Cleric, Rogue, Wizard, and Fighter, and cards for species, backgrounds, spells, and gear so nobody has to build a character from scratch. Three to five players run through three adventure booklets split between combat, exploration, and roleplaying, and the poster maps for the Keep and the Caves of Chaos pull from one of the oldest modules in the game’s history. If you haven't played the Horrified series, it's worth checking out for team-based beast-slaying. Players join forces to take on various classic monster — in this version it's American monsters that include Bigfoot, the Jersey Devil, and Mothman — with different ways of killing each monster. Board game fans will be familiar with the mechanics of the gameplay but the great thing about it is that you can mix and match the monsters, so each time you play is different. It can also get pretty tense as you ratchet up the difficulty level. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • Beyond skin rejuvenation, clinical studies suggest red-light therapy can help energize hair follicles, increase blood circulation in the scalp, reduce inflammation, and lower dihydrotestosterone levels—a hormone that causes hair loss and thinning.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that hair loss isn’t always dramatic. It can be incremental. You start noticing a bit more scalp in harsh bathroom lighting, a tiny bald spot when you tie your hair up in a ponytail. The shower drain is more clogged than usual. Not long ago, hair-loss treatments meant topical remedies, supplements, or a flight to Turkey. Luckily, red-light therapy brings the potential for hair regrowth into your home—no clinical appointment required.

Beyond skin rejuvenation, clinical studies suggest red-light therapy can help energize hair follicles, increase blood circulation in the scalp, reduce inflammation, and lower dihydrotestosterone levels—a hormone that causes hair loss and thinning. Red-light therapy also supports adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, which helps provide oxygen and blood flow to the scalp and triggers follicles to remain in the hair growth phase.

Industry observers note that to determine the best red-light therapy for hair growth, I tapped five WIRED tech reviewers who've dealt with hair loss themselves. We assessed red-light caps, hands-free helmets with full scalp coverage, and low-level laser therapy (LLLT) or photobiomodulation devices for 16 weeks. Along the way, I reviewed the research, spoke with dermatologists, and tracked ease of use. These are the favorites that produced meaningful results and earned our trust.

Be sure to check out our other wellness and skin-care guides, including the Best LED Masks, Best Hair Dryers, and Best Blow Dry Brushes.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

In a recent development, updated November 2026: I added the Capillus HairBand to Honorable Mentions, and I included a product to avoid. Prices, links, and product information were also updated.

To start, I consulted board-certified dermatologists and referred to clinical trials to help determine what features to look for when shopping for a device. I test these devices with several tech reviewers on our team, all of whom have personal experience with hair thinning or loss to different degrees. Most of these at-home gadgets call for a 16-week treatment cycle. We follow the brands' directions and record any visible results along the way.

In a recent development, we monitor changes in hair count, hair density, and scalp health, but effectiveness is only one of the factors we consider. We also judge ease of use, functionality, and comfort. We note the specific wavelengths of light and whether the treatment options feel tolerable or difficult to integrate into everyday routines.

Industry observers note that we also prioritize safety, checking for FDA clearance, automatic shut-off features, and overall durability of the design. To date, our testers have not experienced any side effects, but we would have documented them had they.

I'm testing the Foreo Flip Play and the Theradome PRO Laser Hair Growth Helmet LH80.

Recent findings suggest that currentBody's LED Hair Growth Helmet is a wearable, cord-free, Bluetooth-enabled device designed to improve hair density, thickness, and overall condition. After 12 weeks, I didn’t notice a difference in hair length—I did get a haircut halfway through testing—but I did spot upcoming follicles sprouting along my scalp and sideburn area. My hairstylist mentioned that my hair felt thicker, and I noticed less breakage and hair caught in bristles when brushing. My balding roommate also tested the CurrentBody helmet, and he noted that his hair also felt thicker and that there was new growth around the scalp.

In a recent development, the circular earmuffs protect sensitive ears with a cushy, removable faux leather cloth, and they can be adjusted several inches up or down to ensure a comfortable fit. You can also connect the device to Bluetooth and play any type of audio during sessions, because God forbid I be left alone with my thoughts for 10 minutes a day. My only complaint is that the ear covers aren’t the easiest to adjust and would oftentimes pull out my hair when I removed the helmet. Nevertheless, this is the best red-light therapy for fuller hair. See my full review here. —Molly Higgins.

At first glance, the HigherDose Red Light Hat looks like your everyday baseball cap, with a brand logo embroidered across the top—until you notice the little battery cap and controller on the back, or the 120 LED light bulbs lining the inside. While I don’t suffer from natural hair loss, I’ve struggled with trichotillomania since my teens. Part of what initiated the habit is that any time my sensitive scalp gets irritated, the itchiness drives me to pull at the hair around the spot. But in the months I’ve been using the HigherDose hat, I have felt like my scalp has been happier, with fewer irritated spots and overall itchiness, leaving me less likely to reach for my scalp. Last October, after my first month with this device, my hairstylist saw healthier regrowth instead of the breakage she usually sees. In January, she took another look and noted that my usual problem spot on the back of my head had grown in better than ever. She didn’t find any reaction on my scalp, either, from four months of using the device, and my roots look thicker all around my head.

Similar to my infrared brushes, I find that my hair is a tad oilier after use; both types of devices employ infrared light that can lock in moisture. It’s not a problem on days when my hair is clean, but if my hair is already dirty, using this hat requires an immediate shower. Overall, though, using the HigherDose hat has had a serious payoff for me, my scalp, and my hair. See my full review here. —Nena Farrell.

In a recent development, I seem to rival a golden retriever in terms of shedding, and my sensitive scalp makes things itchy and flaky. To nip it in the bud, I tested the iRestore Elite device, along with the Max Growth kit. It sits right on the crown of your head, and it does heat up quite a bit as the red light puts focused emphasis on your scalp. The red-light exposure has helped prevent flare-ups, as I have none to note from my time testing it. That’s a feat in itself.

However, I’m not the success story here. I recruited a balding tester (my husband, who also gets to give products a spin) who wanted to give it a go to see if it would help with his receding hairline. After three months of consistent use, his hair density has bounced back significantly. It’s a regular sight to see him drink his morning coffee while waiting for the Elite’s 12-minute run time to wrap up. The accompanying Max Growth hair products smell wonderful, and they also played a contributing role in his follicular blossoming. Now, if only he would stop taking them out of my shower. See my full review here. —Julia Forbes.

Unlike other devices on this list, GroWell is designed to be used every other day rather than every day to give your scalp a rest day to process the cellular stimulation (photobiomodulation). Also, unlike others, its wattage is limited to avoid oversaturating follicles past what studies show is the optimal 3 to 4 joules. What GroWell does do is treat your scalp with a proprietary combination of lasers and LEDs to create a blanket of energy you can feel lightly warming your scalp. (GrowWell's therapy-grade laser and LED diodes are proprietary to Apira, the tech giant behind iGrow and GroWell, and are not the same as the generic diodes common in lower-end caps sold online.) The other major difference—which I would call a massive advantage—is separating those lasers from a bulky device. Instead, the GroWell is a flat pad that fits inside a baseball hat. There are hats included in the packaging, and I use them when I'm home. But this product is hassle-free to travel with (it takes up as much room as a pair of socks), and you can tuck it into any normal ball cap on a trip where you're flying carry-on only.

I've been using the laser cap for two months and have grown my always-thin and fine hair out for the first time in 15 years. It's worked well enough that I'm not asked as many questions about it as you might expect—everyone assumes I just shaved my head purely by choice now that they see me with a pretty regular amount of hair for a middle-aged guy. See my full rave here. —Martin Cizmar.

Industry observers note that laduora Duo 4-in-1 Red Light Therapy Scalp and Hair Care Device for $300: The Laduora Duo combines red-light therapy, microcurrent stimulation, sonic vibrations, and thermotherapy into one hairbrush-like device. Sources indicate that hooga Red Light Therapy Hat for Hair Growth for $299: I was excited to try this more affordable red-light hat after loving my experience with the HigherDose one, but I found myself unimpressed and actually uncomfortable while using it. Feels a little pointless to look outdoor-ready when you can’t actually use it on the go. It also got too hot for me to wear comfortably. —Nena Farrell.

Does Red-Light Therapy Work for Hair Loss?

According to recent reports, yes—research suggests low-level light therapy can work for certain types of hair loss, such as androgenetic alopecia, also known as male or female pattern hair loss. It can help increase hair count, thickness, and density by stimulating hair follicles and boosting cellular activity in the scalp.

Industry observers note that that mentioned, results depend heavily on the type and severity of hair loss. Red-light therapy works best in cases of mild to moderate thinning and may be less effective for advanced hair loss or scarring conditions like cicatricial alopecia. Consistency also matters. You typically need regular, ongoing use to maintain results, and benefits can diminish if treatments stop.

What Wavelength of Red Light Is Best for Hair Restoration?

According to the American Hair Loss Association, wavelengths in the range of 630 to 680 nanometers are ideal for hair regrowth. These wavelengths are known to support increased blood flow to the scalp, boost cellular activity, and help reduce inflammation. Some clinical studies specifically cite 650 nanometers as an especially effective wavelength.

Recent findings suggest that red-light devices that use medical-grade laser diodes tend to deliver more targeted and consistent light than standard LEDs, but both can stimulate hair follicles at the right wavelengths. For best results, look for FDA-cleared devices that list their wavelengths and power output.

How to Use Red-Light Therapy for Hair Growth.

In a recent development, consistency is the most important part of any red-light therapy routine. Most devices require at least three months of use before noticeable results are observed, and some may take longer. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions, as treatment schedules vary by device, but most recommend sessions three to five times per week. The hair growth is preserved only with continued use, so you’ll need ongoing maintenance sessions.

According to recent reports, always start with a clean and dry scalp so the light can reach your hair follicles without interference from oils or styling products. Some devices include protective eyewear, and if yours does, wear it during treatment. Make sure to wipe the device down with a gentle disinfectant before or after each session to prevent buildup on the LEDs.

In a recent development, topical regrowth treatments can complement red-light therapy and may help support thicker hair. A few randomized clinical trials suggest that combining minoxidil (2 percent or 5 percent) with red-light therapy can improve hair density and encourage faster regrowth compared to using either treatment alone. For a natural alternative, some research has found rosemary oil to produce results comparable to 2 percent minoxidil for androgenetic alopecia, though the evidence isn’t as extensive as it is for minoxidil.

If you’re pregnant or have an underlying medical condition, talk to your healthcare provider before starting any form of red-light therapy.

Is Red-Light Therapy for Hair Growth Safe?

According to recent reports, yes—for most people, red-light therapy is considered a safe and noninvasive treatment with minimal side effects when used as intended. Still, it's always worth consulting a health care professional before starting any sort of treatment. This is especially the case for anyone with photosensitive conditions or autoimmune disorders that affect light sensitivity.

Industry observers note that I prefer devices that are FDA-cleared because it means they've met certain safety standards for consumer use. But keep in mind that the clearance process is less rigorous than the FDA approval pathway, as it just requires manufacturers to prove their product is “substantially equivalent” to an already legally marketed device. Also, FDA clearance isn't a guarantee of results; it simply means it's considered safe to use as directed at home.

The 6 Best Latte Machines for Automatic Espresso Drinks (2026)

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A latte is rich and milky heaven.
  • Some machines make it easy and keep you from having to drive to the coffee shop.
  • It has been revealed that most of the machines on this list also come with grinders, but our guide to The Best Coffee Grinders may also be helpful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A latte is rich and milky heaven. A cappuccino is the cloud that heaven rests on. The best latte machines and the best automatic espresso machines are the ones that can give you this richness consistently, easily, and deliciously. Home espresso machines, like the classic devices in our guide to the Best Espresso Machines, often have a reputation for being intimidating. But they don't have to be.

Some machines make it easy and keep you from having to drive to the coffee shop. The automatic espresso machines in this guide can make a perfect frothy cappuccino accessible with the press of a single button, or maybe a couple of buttons. Our top high-end superautomatic espresso machine, the De'Longhi Rivelia (7/10, WIRED Recommends), is a paragon of easy-peasy, frothy, pleasing cappuccinos and flat whites. The latest Ninja Cafe Luxe Pro (see here on Amazon) seems determined to produce every kind of coffee in existence.

It has been revealed that most of the machines on this list also come with grinders, but our guide to The Best Coffee Grinders may also be helpful. For more WIRED coffee coverage, check out our guides to The Best Coffee Subscriptions, The Best Drip Coffee Machines, The Best Milk Frothers, and The Best Cold Brew Makers, or look for our recent coffee gear reviews.

Updated November 2026: We’ve added information on WIRED UK’s blind taste test of popular fully automatic bean-to-cup machines and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

A sophisticated bean-to-cup machine from Italian coffee titan De'Longhi, the Rivelia (7/10, WIRED Recommends) immediately ranks among the most modern, impressive, user-friendly, and capable superautomatic espresso machines I’ve encountered—the sort that has you dump a half-bag of beans into a hopper and will grind, brew, then froth up milk for a flat white, amid 18 options on espresso, latte, cappuccino, and iced-coffee drink options.

Industry observers note that pretty much everything operates via an easy touchscreen, including bean guidance that lets you optimize the machine for each bean. The milk frother works at the press of a button and makes actual microfoam—and the foam’s density can be adjusted to make a frothier cappuccino or dense flat white. It’s so easy I let my parents test-drive it, and they fell in love with it within a day. If you’ve got multiple people using the machine, you can save multiple profiles and your favorite custom drinks. So Dad can have his basic “coffee” that’s actually a European-style café crema, and Mom can have her ridiculously large 16-ounce travel-mug latte. (Yes, these are their drinks.).

Industry observers note that what's better, the Rivelia has two swappable bean hoppers, so it’s easy to swap between caff and decaf, or between light and dark roasts. Honestly, this is the bean-to-cup espresso machine that fully sold me on the idea of automatic coffee machines like this one. Though note: Fully automatic espresso machines like the Rivelia grind a little coarser, in order to make espresso less finicky and less difficult. This leads to a smoother but less nuanced profile than espresso shots you’d find in a café. But if you're a milk lover, the absolute ease with which the Rivelia froths a cappuccino will likely balance this out. The cold espresso is also a pleasant option when mixed with milk or vodka.

A lot of machines can make you a cloudy, clumpy, massive-bubble cappuccino without much hassle. But it's that well-integrated microfoam, the silkiness, that feels like an actual luxury—elevates a good foamed milk from the merely milky latte to silly morning ecstasy.

Recent findings suggest that there's a lot to like about Ninja's flagship entry into the espresso market: in particular, dosing by weight and an easy bean guidance function that actually helps in dialing in a bean. Quite simply, this machine offers real-deal, unpressurized portafilter espresso without the fussiness. But what I especially like about this Ninja is the milk. Some superautomatic machines have tube-filled, plasticky milk systems that are annoying to clean. Some never get a fine froth. This Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro is the best of each world, a steam wand and stainless steel steamer cup with a spinning whisk at its bottom that simulates the whirlpool created by a skilled barista. Whether cold foam or hot foam, Ninja's Luxe Cafe series offers truly excellent foam for your morning cup.

Industry observers note that now, for this: It is not a superautomatic machine like the Rivelia, though it’s among the easiest portafilter machines I've ever used. The conical burr grinder is built in, it doses accurately, the tamper handle is easy, and bean guidance will tell you what to do without much fuss. Mostly, you just need to transfer the portafilter from one spot on the machine to another.

Industry observers note that note that for a lower price, the Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier (described below) offers the same great milk froth, but you lose the automatic tamper and a hot water spout. For me, the Pro is the pick for a more pleasant morning and greater versatility. Note that while the massive drip tray does hold a lot of water, it’s a bit of a production to empty and replace, and that while it also purports to be a drip coffee maker, it’s nothing to write your mother about.

Industry observers note that this Mr. Coffee machine was once our top pick for lattes. Why? Because it sits so nicely at a comfortable intersection where ease of use meets automation and affordability. This is about the lowest-priced machine you can ever expect to find with automatic milk frothing at the press of a single button, with options for latte foam or cappuccino froth. Just load fine-ground coffee into the portafilter, tamp it down, and twist it on. The machine will mix up a cappuccino or a latte macchiato at the press of a button.

This machine has a forgiving (but not overly intense or nuanced) pressurized portafilter, which means it will work with almost any “espresso-grind” coffee from your local café or the grocery store. Just note you’ll still get a better shot of espresso if you buy a grinder and use fresh beans from a good specialty roaster. But all in all, this is about the easiest $200 latte machine we know. Like, the hardest thing about it is that the milk canister can be removed and stored in the fridge, and you have to clean it out once a week.

The Cafe Affetto is one of the few fully automatic machines that WIRED has enjoyed in this price range. The Affetto features a built-in steaming wand, produces 20 bars of pump pressure to ensure your espresso is fully extracted, and is a slick little machine. It’s very slim and fits comfortably on a small apartment countertop without having to rearrange everything. Because coffee production is automated, you just need to fill the water tank and put whole beans in the hopper, and you’re good to go. You can brew one or two shots with just the press of a button, and there’s a programmable button to create your favorite drinks (like an Americano with just the right amount of water).

The milk frother does a lot of the work on its own. Just pour some of your favorite milk into the frothing pitcher, submerge the wand, and hit the steam button. If you’re upcoming to frothing milk, you don't even need to move the pitcher to produce a creamy and consistent microfoam. WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey tested the frother with dairy milk, oat milk, and soy milk, and found it produced soft and creamy café-grade froth each time. Just make sure it’s topped up with water and beans and that you clean out the spent grounds container regularly, and it works like a dream.

Industry observers note that the Breville Oracle Jet (8/10, WIRED Recommends) is my favorite of the two dozen or so newly introduced espresso machines I’ve tried so far this year. It’s the one I recommend as my top pick in WIRED’s guide to the Best Espresso Machines, over other estimable contenders from Breville that include the Barista Touch ($1,000) and the Barista Pro ($850). And it’s the one that best mixes full-flavored, nuanced espresso with the ease of machine-guided, touchscreen operation. It’s versatile, it’s powerful, its PID controller means the brew temperature is quite stable, and it makes absolutely lovely cups—espresso that’s denser and more intensely aromatic than the coffee made by any other machine on this list, whether in bringing out the fruity berry notes in an anaerobic light roast or the dark chocolate of a roasty Italian.

According to recent reports, in the finicky, often difficult world of classic home espresso machines, the Oracle Jet is a paragon of simplicity and machine-guided brewing: It’s a miracle that one can so easily pull such delicious and nuanced shots that remain so sensitive to the character of each bean. But that sensitivity still makes the Oracle Jet a little more finicky than other machines on this list. And while the automatic milk frothing is quite good, it’s not as failsafe as our favorites here. (I still like steaming milk manually on the Breville, versus using the auto-froth.).

Which is to say that as a latte machine, this Breville is all about the espresso. If you want espresso that will distill the beauteous character of fresh-roasted beans but still don't want to try overly hard—on a machine whose intuitive touchscreen tutorial will guide you to lovely flat whites and capps? This is your huckleberry.

Sources indicate that for those who’d rather not fuss with beans at all but still want a lovely milk-frothed latte and cappuccino in the morning, there is this clever two-piece setup from Nespresso—with “espresso” on one machine via Vertuo coffee pods and an Aeroccino milk frother that’s whisper-quiet and will whip you up some milk foam in a minute. The espresso that comes from pods is not quite espresso, of course, but WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe loved it best of all pod espresso machines, with excellent body and mouthfeel and especially ease. The Vertuo Pop+ will also make a drip-coffee-style mug.

But this frother bundle generally offers you a good bargain on an all-in-one system, and the Aeroccino is in the upper echelon of milk frothers WIRED has tested. (Note, however, you'll have to plug in each machine separately.) This remarked, if you want the ease of pod espresso but are fussy about your milk, you may want to grab a stand-alone Vertuo Pop+ ($129) and the excellent Dreo Baristamaker ($100). Do this when a good sale is running, and you might cobble this together at a similar price to the Aeroccino bundle.

It has been revealed that the Aeroccino was easy to use—pour in your milk of choice and press the button. it will heat and froth your milk automatically—it takes about a minute, and it’s whisper-quiet. Every Nespresso capsule I’ve tried has featured a thick layer of crema, and having whipped, thick milk on top of it made my average cup of coffee a more elevated experience.

According to recent reports, sometimes making a whole latte or cappuccino using an automated machine can be a time suck. Not to mention, sometimes all you really want is frothy milk. That’s where milk frothers come in. These machines beat air into milk, or milk substitutes, to get that nice creamy froth. Former WIRED Reviewer Jaina Grey loved this handheld from Subminimal, a highly specialized immersion blender that makes properly textured, creamy, light, airy, wonderful milk. One screen makes fine-textured milk. One makes “ultra-fine.” Note that Subminimal has also added a milk frothing pitcher called the Nanofoamer Pro ($159) that costs a bit more, but is currently sitting prettily atop our guide to the Best Milk Frothers.

According to recent reports, this streamlined machine from relative newcomer Terra Kaffe is a pleasant surprise, given the complexity of Terra Kaffe's first machine, the superautomatic TK-02 (see below), which bristled with features and doohickeys. The Demi is perhaps the dead-simplest fully automatic espresso machine I've yet encountered that still makes good coffee. If you don't want to customize your shot, there's just a dial and a button: espresso, lungo, Americano, drip, hot water, bye!

According to recent reports, you can click into submenus and edit these to a nerd's content, both by volume and strength. You can adjust among five grinder settings as well—a low but relatively typical number of settings for automatic machines that already grind coarser than espresso machines with portafilters. You may need to futz with grind and dose strength to get good results with light roast, especially on espresso, but with a good medium roast, the Terra Kaffe offers a very smooth ride. Honestly, this is the machine I'd put in a front room for customers to use if I owned a small business. Super easy, no fuss, good for multiple types of people—and the reservoir is substantial enough at 1.4 liters that you won't be refilling the water all day.

It has been revealed that but note that this is actually not a latte machine: It's only half of one. There's no milk frother. Luckily, the world is full of good milk frothing jugs these days, and we especially recommend the Subminimal Nanofoamer Pro ($159), WIRED's favorite milk frother.

Ninja has a habit of taking high-falutin', pro-level, or commercial equipment—whether soft-serve ice cream machines or slushie machines—and finding a way to make it easy, accessible, fun, and probably viral on TikTok. WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane was skeptical about Ninja's first foray into the latte and cappuccino world with the Luxe Cafe Premier (7/10, WIRED Recommends), especially since the machine also promised cold brew and even traditional drip coffee. But she came away impressed.

This Ninja is not a superautomatic machine like our top automated pick, the Rivelia. It's what the industry likes to call “semiautomatic.” Semiautomatic espresso machines offer a built-in grinder and automatic milk frother but still use a non-pressurized portafilter that will pull a classic espresso shot with full nuance and aromatics. In our espresso maker guide, we recommend the ever-reliable and terrific Breville Barista Express ($700) as WIRED's favorite accessibly priced semiautomatic. But this Ninja is the machine I'd probably give to a beginner, a new college grad, or anyone whose first priority is ease and great automatically foamed milk.

Industry observers note that the drip coffee is meh, granted. But more than perhaps any semiautomatic machine in its price range, the Ninja Cafe Luxe Premier is geared to absolute ease and versatility—with an intuitive digital user interface that helps you along. Depending on your chosen drink, the Ninja Luxe will recommend the appropriate grind size on its display screen and help you dial it in. (This may take a couple of tries.) Milk frothing is easy, and the automatic milk frothing is shockingly good. Plus, you can froth cold foam, for silly cold-foam drinks. See what I mean? Ninja is fun. That said, we ended up preferring the Luxe Cafe Pro ($750), which costs a little more but adds a welcome auto-tamper and hot water spout.

Amazon (with attached milk carafe).

Recent findings suggest that this superautomatic espresso machine is one of the few coffee machines made by German auto and appliance behemoth Bosch. It is both highly sophisticated and a bit of an odd duck—capable of making an unholy variety of espresso drinks downloaded via firmware. The milk system is especially interesting, and for some, it may be the biggest selling point. On the base model, the milk system is basically a tube you attach to the side of the brew head. You can stick the other end of the tube in any container, and it'll steam whatever milk you've got directly into your cup before adding the espresso. This is great for families who use multiple milks. It's also great for not wasting milk.

The espresso is similar to superautomatics from De'Longhi, which is to say it's a smoother, more rounded, but less nuanced take on espresso that's great for milk drinks. But the “drip” is also interesting. The Bosch 800 “slow brew” coffee—while it does not have the clarity or brightness of drip coffee— is perhaps my favorite drip coffee from an espresso machine, round and roasty and lovely. It extracts only the smooth, chocolate end of the coffee spectrum. I haven't tested the pH, but it seems quite low in acidity. It's nice.

In a recent development, but here are the caveats: Coffee cup height clearance can be an problem on milk drinks, the pump is a bit louder than some, it's slow to boot up, and some parts feel a bit flimsy or plasticky for a machine in this price range. Also, if you do want an attached milk carafe, it's hundreds of dollars more, depending on current deals.

It has been revealed that the delta between home espresso machines and the commercial workhorses used by busy third-wave shops is still thousands of dollars, but that hasn’t stopped both beloved brands and scrappy upstarts from infiltrating the space with more approachable units. Skip the junk and level up to the Casabrews 5700PRO (7/10, WIRED Review), which offers an unfussy take on the art of homemade espresso drinks.

Sources indicate that instead of bewildering noobs with a million settings and onboard tutorials, this 12 x 11 x 16-inch tank of a machine keeps it simple with easily accessible controls for things like temperature and dose volume for extraction, and run time for the onboard grinder. It's a single-boiler machine, not a dual boiler, which means you can’t froth your latte milk at the same time as pulling a shot, but the texture of the frothed milk is perfectly malleable and up to snuff for a basic leaf or rosetta pattern.

Recent findings suggest that the guide rails that hold the portafilter in place are a bit too close to the output spout of the grinder, and temperature controls that deal in absolute rather than relative values would be welcome improvements. But until Casabrews implements our feedback, this is still a solid unit that’s a great pick for anyone who’s ready to never leave their house for a cappuccino ever again. —Pete Cottell.

Industry observers note that the superautomatic Terra Kaffe is a pricey hunk of machinery and has its bugs, but considering its ease and customizability, it's worth the price, wrote WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane last year. She praised the device's convenience, its ease, the front-facing water filter, waste tray, and milk carafe, and its excellent app (available for iOs and Android) that offers easy controls and the ability to warm up your machine from your bed or the bathroom.

According to recent reports, drinks like latte macchiatos, drips, and iced coffee can all be adjusted to your tastes, and a milk frothing dial allows you to adjust the milk’s texture from foamy to silky. For those who love true, real, drip coffee, that's the biggest selling point for the Terra Kaffe over our top automated picks, the De'Longhi Rivelia and the Ninja Cafe Luxe Premier: The TK-02 offers it. The drip coffee is also good enough that Shane cleared her Chemex pour-over carafe from her counter.

Industry observers note that de’Longhi’s Magnifica Start is a no-nonsense superautomatic with a conical burr grinder, four preset recipes at the push of a button, and the ability to brew a smooth and potent espresso, wrote WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane. As with other high-end De'Longhi devices of the moment, the milk frother is truly impressive, offering seriously luxurious frothed milk. Milk-based recipes at the touch of a button are a latte macchiato and a cappuccino, while espresso and Americanos are the espresso-based options. There’s a slot for ground beans and a hopper for whole beans. Figuring out grind size takes a little trial and error, Shane noted, and it's not an overly quiet machine. But the Start is compact and efficient, and priced far lower than our favorite De'Longhi automatic, the Rivelia. This makes the Magnifica Start a solid investment.

According to recent reports, the key here is automation. We wanted to test machines that make you a cup of coffee with a single touch, or as close to that as possible. So the products on this list are all of the automatic and semiautomatic variety. You fill ’em up and they do all the hard work—or most of it, anyway. Nothing here doesn't have a milk frother that does the work by itself.

Sources indicate that setup and cleanup were especially key, as was durability. The entire point of a device like this is to save time and energy and/or produce a drink of higher quality than can be made without it, so we didn’t recommend any products that didn’t produce tasty espresso and save time.

In May 2026, WIRED’s UK team gathered four fully automatic machines—the Terra Kaffe TK-02 (above), Philips’ Café Aromis 8000 Series, De'Longhi's Eletta Explore, and Jura E8—and made both lattes and espressos for local industry experts to judge. You can read the results and watch the resulting video here. The Reviews team is currently testing the winner of that challenge, Philips Café Aromis 8000, to see how it compares against the top picks in this guide.

Even if you're not making espresso, the first and best thing you can do to dramatically improve your morning coffee is to buy locally roasted beans. Plug your city or region and “locally roasted coffee beans” into Google and you will be glad you did. The reason that your locally roasted coffee will taste worlds better than anything you'd buy from a major coffee roaster (like Starbucks, Illy, or Gevalia) is simple: Good coffee starts to lose flavor the moment it's roasted. Get it fresh and you're giving yourself a much better chance at high-quality espresso.

According to recent reports, want some help finding the best roasters? For some of our favorite mail-order brands, with beans often roasted the same day or week they're placed in the mail, check out our roundup of the Best Coffee Subscription Services.

It has been revealed that I hate to break it to you, but pre-ground coffee from a supermarket bag is pretty much always worse. Unless you see a roasting date on the bag, you probably have no idea when the roaster actually roasted it. If the roaster is a French or Italian brand, there's a good chance it was months ago. Coffee is best when it's fresh, ideally brewed a week or two after it's roasted. And grinding the beans dramatically increases the rate at which coffee degrades. This doesn't just affect how the coffee tastes. It affects how well the espresso maker will push water through the beans, leading to possible blowouts or bad extraction.

It has been revealed that if you haven’t made espresso before and you don't have access to a coffee grinder, we recommend you buy locally roasted beans. Just ask your local coffee roaster for a fine (espresso) grind. We've tried a lot of pre-ground espresso blends from popular companies like Lavazza, Gevalia, and Café Bustelo. They were all very dark and very bitter, partially because they are all either imported or roasted in big batches and shipped all over the world. Pre-ground coffee will always be a little stale, and it's hard to get a good cup from coffee that's started to degrade—which happens fast after you grind it.

Get it ground fresh from a local roaster, and you'll have about a two-week window before you'll notice any difference. Many of the machines recommended here come with a grinder, so whole beans are already the best choice. But our roundup of The Best Coffee Grinders can also provide some guidance here, if you want to get into the grinding game, buy whole beans, and keep your coffee tasting its best.

Look, milk is milk. Anything that contains milk has the potential to get strange over time, and this includes the milk containers and milk frothers on automatic espresso machines. WIRED's previous espresso reviewer, Jaina Grey, was extremely sensitive to this issue—devoting her time to dishwashering, soaping, scrubbing, and otherwise testing the best methods for making sure that milk containers on automatic espresso machines remain sacrosanct environments.

Industry observers note that regular washing is, of course, the first and best recourse. But occasionally, you'll also want to sterilize your milk reservoir and milk frother.

Recent findings suggest that first, hand-wash it with soap and water as usual, and make sure you get a sponge into those corners. Next up, there are a couple of options. The most effective will be a food-grade sanitizer like Star San, or One Step. Essentially, just make a dilution per the instructions on either product, pour that into a spray bottle, give the inside of the milk container a couple of sprays, and let it dry on a drying rack.

The second-best option, the one that uses things you probably have in your house right now, is a mix of distilled white vinegar and plain old tap water. If you have staining or really stubborn smells, you'll want to let it soak. Try adding about one shot glass (1.5 ounces) of distilled white vinegar and fill the container up the rest of the way with warm water. Let it soak for about 30 minutes, then rinse it out till there's no more vinegar smell, and you should be good to go.
